ocar.opportunity: Small recurrent subgraphs (motifs) can fingerprint how a nervous system is organized, including when connections sit in separate molecular layers rather than a single mixed graph.
ocar.challenge: The C. elegans connectome is multi-layer (gap junctions plus chemically distinct synapses), so motif counts on an aggregated graph can hide layer-specific structure, and random graphs of the same size and density are needed as a null.
ocar.action: Sharma, Renz, and Hövel, in European Physical Journal B (2024), apply the ESCAPE subgraph-counting algorithm to 3-, 4-, and 5-node motifs in individual layers, the aggregated network, and the locomotory circuit, comparing counts to an ensemble of 1000 random networks with matched node and link counts.
ocar.resolution: For almost all layers and motif types, motif occurrence cannot be explained by the random model. Wedges, closed-path motifs (triangles, 4- and 5-cycles), and hub-and-spoke stars are abundant; 4-cycles and diamonds recur across layers. 3-path and 4-path motifs are insignificant in the electrical and GABA layers, and 4- and 5-cliques are less prominent.
ocar.future_work: The authors propose fingerprinting other empirical networks, swapping in different null models, using motif composition to inform generative simulations, and counting motifs whose links sit in different layers so cross-layer pathways become visible.

summaries.beginner: The worm C. elegans has a complete wiring diagram that can be split by synapse type. This paper counts small repeating wiring patterns in each layer and shows that most of those patterns are not what you would get from a random network of the same size.
summaries.intermediate: In European Physical Journal B (2024), Sharma, Renz, and Hövel use ESCAPE to count 3-, 4-, and 5-node motifs in the multi-layer C. elegans connectome, including electrical and transmitter-specific synaptic layers, the aggregated graph, and the locomotory circuit. Significance is judged against 1000 density-matched random networks. They report conserved wedge motifs (shared regulators), closed-path motifs consistent with feedback, and hub-and-spoke stars, while 3-path and 4-path motifs fail to characterize the electrical and GABA layers and fully connected 4- and 5-cliques are relatively rare.
summaries.advanced: Significance is relative to Erdős–Rényi-style random graphs of matched size and density, not degree-preserving or spatial nulls; the authors themselves flag other null classes as future work. Motif names (wedge, diamond, clique) are graph-theoretic, not physiological identifications. Counts of more complex 5-node motifs drop in small layers, so absence can reflect size. The extract’s discussion does not report a single numeric enrichment score for the whole connectome.

plain_language_summary: The worm C. elegans has a complete wiring diagram that can be split by synapse type. This paper counts small repeating wiring patterns in each layer and shows that most of those patterns are not what you would get from a random network of the same size.

ocar.opportunity: Connectomic EM volumes are already petabyte-scale and heading toward exascale whole-mouse collections, so storage and transfer are becoming a bottleneck even as imaging and analysis improve.
ocar.challenge: Standard codecs such as AVIF and JPEG2000 introduce merge and split errors in membrane and instance segmentation as compression increases, so a method must shrink data without destroying features used for tracing.
ocar.action: Li, Park, Xenes, Bishop, Berger, Samuel, Wester, Lichtman, Pfister, Li, and Meirovitch present EM-Compressor on bioRxiv (2024): variational autoencoders trained on human cortical EM (H01) plus a cloud visualization app.
ocar.resolution: On H01 they report compression to as little as 1/128th of the original size without significantly compromising subsequent segmentation, outperforming standard size-reduction methods at 16×, 32×, and 64× in qualitative membrane and instance tests. In VAE feature space, larger spatial resolution is generally more favorable than more channels for high-fidelity neural segmentation.
ocar.future_work: They suggest 3D VAEs or segmentation-optimized models for still higher rates, but warn that volumetric VAEs may not suit all connectomics applications because of the need for near-perfect 3D alignment.

summaries.beginner: Brain electron-microscope movies are so large that storing them is becoming a problem. This team trains a neural compressor that can shrink human cortex images to as little as one 128th of the original size while still allowing computers to find cell membranes.
summaries.intermediate: Posted on bioRxiv (2024), Li and colleagues introduce EM-Compressor, a VAE-based codec evaluated on the H01 human EM volume. They report reduction to as little as 1/128th of original size without significantly harming later segmentation, and qualitative comparisons at 16×, 32×, and 64× against AVIF and JPEG2000, which increasingly produce merge and split errors. A cloud app supports on-the-fly visualization. They also report that, in VAE feature space, larger spatial resolution tends to beat more channels for segmentation fidelity.
summaries.advanced: The 1/128 figure is the most aggressive rate claimed; the extract’s qualitative figure uses 16×–64×. Segmentation quality is described as not significantly compromised rather than as a single F-score. Evaluation is on H01 human cortex, not whole-mouse or fly volumes. Volumetric extension is explicitly cautioned against where 3D alignment must stay near-perfect. The work is a preprint.

plain_language_summary: Brain electron-microscope movies are so large that storing them is becoming a problem. This team trains a neural compressor that can shrink human cortex images to as little as one 128th of the original size while still allowing computers to find cell membranes.

ocar.opportunity: Petascale EM and X-ray microtomography volumes can reveal neural structure and synapses, but only if annotations can be shared, queried, and reused across systems.
ocar.challenge: Without community standards that make volumetric annotations FAIR, costly datasets risk being underused as they grow past petascale and pipelines remain siloed.
ocar.action: Guittari, Wimbish, Rivlin, Hinton, Matelsky, Rose, Rivera, Stock, Wester, Johnson, and Gray-Roncal outline (arXiv.org, 2024, as described in the catalog abstract) a standards framework for annotations originating from high-resolution volumetric imaging and connectomics, coordinated by a global academic–industry working group on EM and XRM pipelines.
ocar.resolution: The stated goal is interoperable annotation management that supports collaboration, more reliable findings, and comparative analysis across species and modalities, considering existing community approaches to neuronal entities, biological components, and metadata.
ocar.future_work: The abstract frames the working group as identifying gaps and refining platforms; it does not report an adopted schema or a completed standard.

summaries.beginner: Huge electron-microscope and X-ray brain maps are expensive to make, and they are hard to reuse if every lab stores labels differently. This paper sketches a shared standards plan so those labels can be found, shared, and compared across tools and species.
summaries.intermediate: Guittari and colleagues (arXiv.org, 2024) outline a FAIR standards framework for annotations on EM and X-ray microtomography connectomic volumes, as described in the catalog abstract. They report forming a global working group with academic and industry partners to identify gaps in current pipelines and to refine platforms for standardizing methods, entities, biological components, and metadata. Summaries here follow the catalog abstract because the associated PDF extract is a different article.
summaries.advanced: The PDF text supplied with pdf_trust=ok is Chen and Parreaux’s compiler paper “The Long Way to Deforestation (Technical Report)” (arXiv:2410.02232), not the Nanoscale Connectomics Annotation Standards Framework. Claims above are taken only from the catalog abstract. Independent reading of the catalog paper is needed for any schema, examples, or working-group deliverables. Do not treat Lumberhack/deforestation results as part of this work.

plain_language_summary: Huge electron-microscope and X-ray brain maps are expensive to make, and they are hard to reuse if every lab stores labels differently. This paper sketches a shared standards plan so those labels can be found, shared, and compared across tools and species.

ocar.opportunity: The fly mushroom body’s Kenyon cells now have a complete synapse-level wiring map, so theoretical point-attractor models of recurrent memory can be tested on real recurrent excitation rather than invented weights.
ocar.challenge: The computational role of Kenyon-cell to Kenyon-cell recurrence has been unclear, and detailed recurrent connectivity in biological populations is usually unknown, so it has been hard to say whether attractor theory maps onto this circuit.
ocar.action: Joyce, Norman-Tenazas, Rivlin, Hwang, Western, Zhang, Gray-Roncal, and Robinson, on bioRxiv (2024), build a connectome-constrained rate model of the mushroom body (ORN→PN→KC, APL, MBON, and KC→KC) from a public hemibrain-style connectome via neuPrint, keeping only connections with more than five synapses inside the mushroom body.
ocar.resolution: Recurrent excitation is highly symmetric and balanced with feedforward input. In simulations it facilitates dimensionality reduction and allows a small set of self-sustaining point-attractor states. The authors sweep recurrent strength to map dynamical regimes and discuss possible functional implications.
ocar.future_work: They suggest the observed relationship between mushroom-body recurrence and point-attractor properties as a base model for comparison with recurrent circuits in other organisms. Reciprocal KC contacts at convergent/rosette synapses were omitted because it is unknown whether activation can propagate there; PN→ORN and MBON→KC feedback were omitted as 1.3% and 1.5% of feedforward synapse counts.

summaries.beginner: Fruit-fly learning cells talk to each other as well as to the next layer. This team builds a computer model from the real wiring map and finds that those extra loops can shrink the activity pattern and hold a few stable “memories.”
summaries.intermediate: Posted on bioRxiv (2024), Joyce and colleagues constrain a mushroom-body network model with synapse counts among ORNs, PNs, Kenyon cells, APL, and MBONs from a public connectome (neuPrint), excluding connections with five or fewer synapses in the mushroom body. They report that Kenyon-cell recurrent excitation is highly symmetric and balanced with feedforward input, that it enables dimensionality reduction and a compact set of self-sustaining point attractors, and that varying recurrent strength explores a range of dynamical regimes.
summaries.advanced: This is a model study, not a new physiology experiment. Attractors are those of the simulated network, not recorded Kenyon-cell states. Rosette reciprocal KC synapses and weak PN→ORN / MBON→KC feedback are omitted by design. The extract’s selected text cuts into methods, so quantitative attractor counts and dimensionality numbers are those stated in the abstract rather than tabulated here. The work is a preprint.

plain_language_summary: Fruit-fly learning cells talk to each other as well as to the next layer. This team builds a computer model from the real wiring map and finds that those extra loops can shrink the activity pattern and hold a few stable “memories.”

ocar.opportunity: Flies must prioritize nearby flies during social behavior, and a connectome can nominate circuit motifs that retune vision when internal state changes.
ocar.challenge: Feature-detecting visual neurons are well mapped, but how attention shifts with goals is much less known, and candidate state-dependent motifs need causal tests.
ocar.action: Schretter, Hindmarsh Sten, Klapoetke, Shao, Nern, Dreher, Bushey, Robie, Taylor, Branson, Otopalik, Ruta, and Rubin, in Nature (2024), use the connectome to identify three motifs poised to change an aggressive female’s response to fly-sized objects, then test them with cell-type-specific genetics, behavior, and physiology; they also examine related circuitry in courting males.
ocar.resolution: The three motifs—convergence of excitatory visual-feature and internal-state inputs, dendritic disinhibition of select feature detectors, and a switch that toggles between two feature detectors—are each used during female aggression. aIPg is the primary sexually dimorphic neuron in the described circuits; LC, lobula interneurons, IB112, and TuTuA are morphologically similar in both sexes. TuTuA activity in males tracking a fictive female, plus the male optic-lobe connectome, suggest the same toggle operates across sexes.
ocar.future_work: The authors argue that multiple motifs give more degrees of freedom for attending to different visual features; mapping how each motif gates distinct motor programs is the implied next step.

summaries.beginner: When a fruit fly is aggressive or courting, it needs to pay extra attention to other flies. This Nature paper uses the wiring diagram to find three circuit tricks that retune vision, then shows they actually work in behaving flies.
summaries.intermediate: In Nature (2024), Schretter and colleagues start from the Drosophila connectome and identify three state-dependent motifs that could modify responses to fly-sized visual objects: excitatory convergence of visual and internal-state inputs, dendritic disinhibition of feature detectors, and a toggle between two feature detectors. Cell-type-specific tools, behavior, and physiology show each motif is used in female aggression, and features of the toggle also operate in male courtship pursuit. They highlight aIPg as the main sexually dimorphic cell in these circuits.
summaries.advanced: The claim that the same toggle operates across sexes rests on male TuTuA recordings during fictive tracking plus male optic-lobe connectome analysis, not a full repeat of the female aggression suite in males. Motif “use” is demonstrated for identified cell types in the extract, not as a brain-wide attention census. The paper is a compelling example of connectome-guided circuit breaking; quantitative synaptic weights and full stimulus sets live in figures not fully captured here.

plain_language_summary: When a fruit fly is aggressive or courting, it needs to pay extra attention to other flies. This Nature paper uses the wiring diagram to find three circuit tricks that retune vision, then shows they actually work in behaving flies.

ocar.opportunity: Genetic circuit tracing could overlay cell identity from single-cell sequencing onto synaptic partners, at throughput that electron microscopy cannot match for plasticity or mutants.
ocar.challenge: EM connectomes are snapshots of one brain, undercount fine neurites, and omit gap junctions and neuromodulation, so they are impractical for asking how connections change over 24 hours or across individuals.
ocar.action: Ehrlich, Xu, Luminari, Kidd, Treiber, Russo, and Blau, on bioRxiv (2024), modify trans-Tango with adult-restricted nuclear reporters so neurons downstream of Drosophila s-LNv clock cells can be purified and sequenced (Tango-seq).
ocar.resolution: s-LNvs preferentially synapse onto a subset of CNMa+ DN1p clock neurons, connections they interpret as likely plastic, and they also find synapses onto mushroom-body Kenyon cells, including a discussion of γ-KC links. The combination supports prior s-LNv→DN2 and s-LNv→DN1p anatomy while adding target specificity.
ocar.future_work: Open questions include the molecular code for choosing CNMa+ DN1ps if the connection is made and broken daily, and whether s-LNv→γ-KC synapses explain circadian rhythms in memory. They recommend adult-restricted trans-Tango ligand expression as part of the toolkit.

summaries.beginner: Electron-microscope wiring maps cannot easily show how a fly’s connections change from day to night. This team tags cells downstream of clock neurons, sequences them, and finds preferred partners among other clock cells and learning-center cells.
summaries.intermediate: Posted on bioRxiv (2024), Ehrlich and colleagues introduce Tango-seq: adult-restricted trans-Tango labeling of neurons synaptically downstream of Drosophila s-LNv clock neurons, followed by nuclear-reporter purification and single-cell sequencing. They report preferential connections to a subset of CNMa+ DN1p neurons, interpreted as likely plastic, and connections to mushroom-body Kenyon cells. They contrast genetic tracing with EM’s single-brain snapshot, synapse undercounting, and lack of gap-junction or neuromodulatory links.
summaries.advanced: Trans-Tango reports proximity/ligand-dependent labeling, not a complete EM-grade synapse census; false partners and missed partners remain possible. “Likely plastic” is an interpretation tied to known s-LNv rhythms, not a time-series connectome in this extract. Sequencing identifies transcriptomic types among labeled cells; quantitative synapse counts versus hemibrain are not given here. The work is a preprint. Flies were raised at 25°C rather than the 18°C sometimes used for strongest trans-Tango, a methods choice noted by the authors.

plain_language_summary: Electron-microscope wiring maps cannot easily show how a fly’s connections change from day to night. This team tags cells downstream of clock neurons, sequences them, and finds preferred partners among other clock cells and learning-center cells.

ocar.opportunity: Volume electron microscopy can list every axon, dendrite, and synapse in a neuropil sample, yielding a local “synaptome” rather than putative light-level contacts.
ocar.challenge: Labeled terminals in light microscopy are only putative synapses, and coarser SBEM voxels can make excitatory versus inhibitory classification and true 3D densities harder.
ocar.action: Turégano-López, de las Pozas, Santuy, Rodríguez, DeFelipe, and Merchán-Pérez, in Communications Biology (2024), skeletonize all nerve fibers in FIB-SEM volumes (5 × 5 × 20 nm³) of mouse hippocampal CA1 stratum radiatum and somatosensory layers 1 and 3, linking each skeleton to synaptic junctions segmented with Espina.
ocar.resolution: They report neuropil packing up to 9 kilometers of fiber per cubic millimeter, plus synapse numbers, fiber lengths, linear synapse densities, and spine-versus-shaft targeting, with statistically significant regional differences (including Chi-square and Kruskal–Wallis tests flagged in figures). Higher resolution versus Motta et al.’s SBEM (11.24 × 11.24 × 28 nm³) is cited as enabling unambiguous excitatory/inhibitory classification without stereological estimation.
ocar.future_work: They position the measurements as inputs for realistic brain models and for comparing normal versus pathological tissue, including human samples.

summaries.beginner: This team traces every nerve fiber in small 3D electron-microscope blocks of mouse hippocampus and cortex. They find the wires are packed extremely tightly—up to about nine kilometers of fiber in a cubic millimeter—and they count how synapses sit on spines versus shafts.
summaries.intermediate: In Communications Biology (2024), Turégano-López and colleagues apply volume EM and custom skeletonization to mouse CA1 stratum radiatum and somatosensory layers 1 and 3. Imaging is FIB-SEM at 5 × 5 × 20 nm³. They report fiber packing up to 9 km per mm³ and quantitative comparisons of excitatory/inhibitory axons, linear synapse densities, and spine-versus-shaft targeting, with regional differences marked significant in the figures. They contrast this resolution with Motta et al.’s SBEM voxel size and argue it supports true synaptic densities rather than stereological estimates.
summaries.advanced: Samples are local neuropil blocks, not whole-area connectomes; “up to 9 km/mm³” is a packing ceiling, not a single number for all regions. Excitatory/inhibitory assignment follows asymmetric versus symmetric ultrastructure as used in cortex. Statistical tests (Chi-square, Kruskal–Wallis/Mann–Whitney with Bonferroni) are reported in figure captions; exact p-values beyond the stated thresholds are not copied here. Human extension is proposed, not shown in this extract.

plain_language_summary: This team traces every nerve fiber in small 3D electron-microscope blocks of mouse hippocampus and cortex. They find the wires are packed extremely tightly—up to about nine kilometers of fiber in a cubic millimeter—and they count how synapses sit on spines versus shafts.

ocar.opportunity: Two- and three-dimensional electron microscopy can localize proteins on neuronal membranes and reconstruct synaptic circuits, including in disease.
ocar.challenge: Conventional TEM is limited in 2D coverage and 3D completeness; volume EM and replica methods are powerful but demanding in sample preparation and analysis time.
ocar.action: Luján, Turégano-López, Aguado, and Merchán-Pérez review, in Advanced Technology in Neuroscience (2024), SDS-digested freeze-fracture replica labeling (SDS–FRL) for 2D protein mapping and volume EM for 3D ultrastructure and connectivity, including five practical SDS–FRL steps.
ocar.resolution: They present SDS–FRL as efficient for large 2D membrane areas with labeling efficiencies that can be close to 100%, and volume EM as enabling 3D visualization beyond single TEM sections, with software evolving to extract connectivity from large datasets. Pathology applications are expected as the methods spread.
ocar.future_work: The review flags ongoing work on faster sample preparation and analysis; it is a methods survey, not a new dataset.

summaries.beginner: Electron microscopes can show both the proteins sitting in a neuron’s membrane and the 3D wiring between cells. This review explains two modern toolkits for those jobs and why they matter for healthy and diseased brains.
summaries.intermediate: In Advanced Technology in Neuroscience (2024), Luján and colleagues review 2D SDS–FRL freeze-fracture immunolabeling and 3D volume electron microscopy for brain ultrastructure. SDS–FRL is described as mapping integral membrane proteins over large areas with labeling efficiencies that can approach 100%, with a five-step protocol (formaldehyde fixation, high-pressure freezing, fracture/replication, SDS cleaning, immunolabeling). Volume EM is framed as extending classical TEM to 3D organelles, cells, and synapses, with dedicated analysis software developing in parallel.
summaries.advanced: This is a review, not a primary reconstruction. “Labeling efficiencies close to 100%” is stated as a capability of SDS–FRL, not a measured result in a specific dataset here. Pathology payoff is prospective. Volume-EM software claims are qualitative. The extract’s later pages are a methods primer rather than a results section.

plain_language_summary: Electron microscopes can show both the proteins sitting in a neuron’s membrane and the 3D wiring between cells. This review explains two modern toolkits for those jobs and why they matter for healthy and diseased brains.

ocar.opportunity: Serial-section scanning EM of the developing cerebellar external granular layer can show mitotic and migratory granule cells in vivo at ultrastructural resolution that live imaging rarely reaches.
ocar.challenge: High-resolution evidence of how progenitors communicate while they divide and migrate has been limited, so putative intercellular bridges could be missed or dismissed as artifacts of one animal or stage.
ocar.action: Cordero Cervantes, Khare, Wilson, Dongo Mendoza, Coulon-Mahdi, Lichtman, and Zurzolo, in Science Advances (2023), reconstruct ssSEM volumes of the cerebellar germinal layer, combining segmentation, 3D reconstruction, and deep learning to find and characterize tunneling intercellular connections (ICs) between granule-cell pairs.
ocar.resolution: ICs are cylindrical cytoplasmic tubes with an electron-dense midbody-like region and microtubules (~25 nm) entering both cells; connected cells are mitotic, migratory, or transitioning, with fully formed nuclei. Preliminary P0 and P3 volumes support ICs not being restricted to one animal or stage. Cargo includes vesicles and membranous compartments.
ocar.future_work: IC numbers per lobule may vary with EGL thickness. Molecular identification of ICs, immunohistochemistry, and fluorescence imaging are proposed to address limitations of EM-only anatomy. A possible role in CNS development remains a hypothesis.

summaries.beginner: In the developing cerebellum, young granule cells were found to be linked by tiny tunnels in 3D electron-microscope reconstructions. The cells on either end can be dividing, migrating, or switching between those jobs.
summaries.intermediate: In Science Advances (2023), Cordero Cervantes and colleagues reconstruct serial-section SEM of the transient cerebellar external granular layer and report anatomically complex intercellular connections between granule-cell pairs. Connected cells span mitotic and migratory states. ICs are defined as cytoplasmic tubes with a midbody-like density and microtubules (~25 nm) into both cells; vesicular and membranous cargo is described. Preliminary P0 and P3 volumes are cited against a single-animal artifact. Code and HAL deposit (pasteur-04065869) accompany the paper.
summaries.advanced: Function is not demonstrated: ICs are structural findings that “pose intriguing hypotheses.” IC incidence may vary by lobule with EGL thickness. Identification criteria (tube shape, midbody-like density, microtubule thickness) are morphological. The selected extract’s later pages are sample-prep methods (ROTO, Epon), so quantitative IC counts per volume are not in this snippet. Deep-learning details of the pipeline are named in the abstract more than specified here.

plain_language_summary: In the developing cerebellum, young granule cells were found to be linked by tiny tunnels in 3D electron-microscope reconstructions. The cells on either end can be dividing, migrating, or switching between those jobs.

ocar.opportunity: Soma locations and shapes in a full adult fly brain from EM would mark neurogenesis origins and support neuron reconstruction, but soma-specific annotations have been missing.
ocar.challenge: Existing deep-learning neuron reconstructions cannot directly give accurate soma maps, and full-brain EM is so large that naive 3D instance segmentation is slow.
ocar.action: Liu, Hu, Li, Huang, Zhang, and Xiong, at CVPR (2023), release EMADS with fine-grained 3D soma labels, a two-stage deep-learning instance segmenter, and a parallel full-brain pipeline, with code and data at github.com/liuxy1103/EMADS.
ocar.resolution: They report benchmark comparisons on a held-out test set claiming superiority of the method, and preliminary biological statistics on reconstructed somas. Figure 5 gives a full-brain total count of 76,316 somas and regional mean sizes/diameters (means marked on histograms, including diameters around 0.47–0.53 μm in the plotted panels).
ocar.future_work: They hope the benchmark aids future Drosophila neural-system studies; the extract does not detail remaining error modes beyond the general difficulty of full-brain scale.

summaries.beginner: Finding every cell body in a fruit-fly electron-microscope brain has been hard because training labels for cell bodies were missing. This CVPR paper adds a labeled dataset, a two-step computer vision method, and a first full-brain soma map.
summaries.intermediate: At CVPR (2023), Liu and colleagues introduce EMADS, a high-resolution EM soma annotation set, and a two-stage 3D instance-segmentation network run with a parallel pipeline on the full adult Drosophila brain. They provide quantitative and qualitative test-set comparisons and biological summary statistics. A figure in the extract reports 76,316 somas in the full brain and regional size and diameter histograms. Code and data are released on GitHub.
summaries.advanced: “One of the first efforts” is an authorship framing. Test-set metric values (F1, IoU) are not in the selected extract, so ranking claims should be checked against the paper’s tables. Soma diameter means in Figure 5 are plotted; treating 76,316 as a biological census assumes segmentation completeness. The IEEE Xplore copy is watermarked as a licensed download. Dataset is fly EM, not a general soma benchmark across species.

plain_language_summary: Finding every cell body in a fruit-fly electron-microscope brain has been hard because training labels for cell bodies were missing. This CVPR paper adds a labeled dataset, a two-step computer vision method, and a first full-brain soma map.

ocar.opportunity: Comparative synaptic connectomics can show whether primate color circuits are conserved despite more than 25 million years of independent evolution among humans, macaques, and marmosets.
ocar.challenge: Macaque and marmoset are standard models of human vision, yet fine-scale foveal wiring—especially short-wavelength (S) cone pathways for blue–yellow vision—might not match humans.
ocar.action: Kim, Packer, Pollreisz, Martin, Grünert, and Dacey, in PNAS (2023), reconstruct S-cone–associated S-ON and S-OFF motifs with connectomic EM in human, macaque, and marmoset foveal retina.
ocar.resolution: Distinctive circuitry arises from S cones in each species. Humans show S-cone contacts with neighboring L and M cones that are rare or absent in macaques and marmosets. Canonical macaque architecture does not hold for human synaptic motifs. Human flat midget bipolar cells consistently bear a Landolt’s club in outer retina, never observed on bipolar cells in macaque or marmoset in this study.
ocar.future_work: The authors suggest the differences may help explain why some aspects of human color perception are not well predicted from macaque physiology; functional recording of the human-specific motifs is outside this anatomy paper.

summaries.beginner: Humans, macaques, and marmosets all see color, but their foveal wiring is not the same. This paper maps the “blue” cone circuit at synapse resolution and finds contacts and cell shapes in humans that the monkey models lack.
summaries.intermediate: In PNAS (2023), Kim and colleagues apply connectomic EM to foveal S-cone pathways in human, macaque, and marmoset. They report species-specific S-cone circuitry, including human S-to-L/M cone contacts that are rare or absent in the monkeys, and a consistent Landolt’s club on human flat midget bipolar cells that was never seen in macaque or marmoset here. They frame the result as evidence that canonical macaque color architecture does not fully predict human synaptic motifs.
summaries.advanced: Sample sizes and reconstructed cone counts live in figures not fully captured in the extract. “Rare or absent” LM contacts in monkeys is qualitative in the selected text. Landolt’s club function is unknown; presence is a morphological species difference. Gap-junction discussion cites ground-squirrel physiology as analogy, not paired human recordings. Comparative claims are for the reconstructed foveal patches, not entire retinas.

plain_language_summary: Humans, macaques, and marmosets all see color, but their foveal wiring is not the same. This paper maps the “blue” cone circuit at synapse resolution and finds contacts and cell shapes in humans that the monkey models lack.

ocar.opportunity: A synapse detector trained in one EM brain region could transfer to another if domain shift can be handled with only weak point labels.
ocar.challenge: Per-dataset training is slow and annotation-heavy, and synapse appearance varies across regions, so a model trained in one volume often fails in another.
ocar.action: Chen, Huang, Zhang, and Xiong present AdaSyn (IEEE ISBI / arXiv, 2023): a two-stage segmentation framework that expands point annotations into masks, trains a 3D SegNet for pre- and postsynaptic channels, regenerates square masks as pseudo-labels on target data, and pairs pre- and post-sites by nearest distance.
ocar.resolution: They report first place in the WASPSYN out-of-domain synapse detection challenge at ISBI 2023. Code is at github.com/qic999/AdaSyn.
ocar.future_work: The extract’s discussion is truncated into the reference list, so remaining error modes and per-volume scores are not in the selected text; generalization beyond the challenge volumes is the implied test.

summaries.beginner: Computers trained to find synapses in one electron-microscope stack often fail on the next brain region. This method uses rough point clicks, adapts to the new images, and won an ISBI 2023 challenge on wasp-brain data.
summaries.intermediate: Chen et al. (IEEE International Symposium on Biomedical Imaging, 2023; arXiv:2308.16461) introduce AdaSyn for domain-adaptive synapse detection from weak point annotations. Stage one expands points and trains a 3D segmentation network with pre- and postsynaptic channels; stage two regenerates square masks as pseudo-labels on the target domain; pairs are matched by nearest distance. They report first place in WASPSYN at ISBI 2023.
summaries.advanced: First-place ranking is a challenge result; numeric F1/precision/recall are not in the selected extract (discussion runs into references). Pseudo-labeling can reinforce errors if stage-one detections are biased. WASPSYN is an out-of-domain microwasp setting; transfer to mammalian cortex is not demonstrated here. Catalog year is 2023 with an ISBI 2024 DOI path; treat venue as the ISBI WASPSYN challenge paper.

plain_language_summary: Computers trained to find synapses in one electron-microscope stack often fail on the next brain region. This method uses rough point clicks, adapts to the new images, and won an ISBI 2023 challenge on wasp-brain data.

ocar.opportunity: Retinal rod pathways under starlight are a minimal pattern-recognition problem (photon detection with little spatial autocorrelation), so their electrical synapses may illustrate a biological pooling layer analogous to convolutional nets.
ocar.challenge: How evolution sized gap-junction pooling in mouse versus macaque, which differ about 7-fold in linear retinal size, needs ultrastructural accounting that light microscopy alone does not provide.
ocar.action: Tsukamoto, in a Frontiers in Cellular Neuroscience perspective (2023), discusses serial-section TEM connectomics of the primary rod pathway in mouse and macaque, with special reference to electrical synapses as a pooling stage, linking that anatomy to CNN-style computation and to membrane tracing practice.
ocar.resolution: The piece argues that ssTEM of small, synapse-rich retinal patches remains useful, that scotopic photon detection is the extreme simplified case of pattern recognition, and that the mouse–macaque size difference can test quantitative design principles of pooling via electrical synapses.
ocar.future_work: The author frames this as a perspective on ongoing comparative work rather than a completed multi-species census; translating pooling anatomy into new algorithms is suggested, not demonstrated.

summaries.beginner: Night vision has to catch single photons and average them without fancy pattern matching. This perspective treats the retina’s electrical synapses as a pooling step like in a convolutional network, comparing mouse and monkey rod pathways.
summaries.intermediate: In Frontiers in Cellular Neuroscience (2023), Tsukamoto offers a perspective linking Neocognitron/CNN history, connectomic membrane classification, and serial-section TEM of mouse and macaque primary rod pathways. Electrical synapses are interpreted as a pooling layer. A roughly 7-fold linear-size difference between mouse and macaque retinas is proposed as a quantitative test of adaptational circuit design under scotopic conditions where spatial autocorrelation is minimal.
summaries.advanced: This is a perspective, not a methods paper with new error rates. The CNN analogy is conceptual. The 7-fold linear-size figure is stated in the abstract as a comparative premise. Discussion pages in the extract mix tracing pedagogy with a conflict-of-interest statement; primary quantitative tables are not in this snippet. Catalog tags include mouse retina ssTEM; macaque is part of the comparison, not a second labeled dataset row.

plain_language_summary: Night vision has to catch single photons and average them without fancy pattern matching. This perspective treats the retina’s electrical synapses as a pooling step like in a convolutional network, comparing mouse and monkey rod pathways.

ocar.opportunity: Voxel segmentation volumes used in scientific visualization can be gigabytes to nearly a terabyte uncompressed, so lossless compression that still supports GPU ray marching would make interactive rendering practical.
ocar.challenge: Many labels and voxels make storage, transfer, and on-the-fly visualization difficult; codecs must decompress fast enough for level-of-detail rendering.
ocar.action: Piochowiak and Dachsbacher, in IEEE Transactions on Visualization and Computer Graphics (2023), encode small bricks by iterative region/boundary refinement, then compress the operation stream with rANS using global frequency tables, enabling parallel (de)compression and GPU rendering with optional brick caching.
ocar.resolution: They report about 1% to 3% of original size, throughput up to gigabytes per second for compression and decompression, and example renderings: 4000 MB → 112 MB (2.8%) at 81 fps; 5694 MB → 51 MB (0.9%) at 62 fps; 927.7 GB → 13.5 GB (1.5%) at 63 fps (1920 × 1080, ray marching with shadows). Brick size b = 64 is a main benchmark setting.
ocar.future_work: Worst-case bricks still compress, but rates vary; the method is evaluated on several fields’ volumes (including connectomics-style label volumes named Cortex, Cells, Fiber in figures).

summaries.beginner: Coloring every voxel in a 3D scan with a cell or material label makes huge files. This paper compresses those label volumes tightly and still draws them in real time on a graphics card.
summaries.intermediate: In IEEE TVCG (2023), Piochowiak and Dachsbacher present lossless brick-wise compression of segmentation volumes: iterative encoding of labeled regions and boundaries, then rANS entropy coding with dataset-wide frequency tables. They report ~1–3% of original size, up to GB/s (de)compression, GPU ray marching with LOD and optional streaming of detail coefficients. Figure examples include 927.7 GB compressed to 13.5 GB (1.5%) at 63 fps. Comparisons include hdf5/gzip, PNG stacks, Compresso, and Neuroglancer.
summaries.advanced: Ratios depend on brick size b and whether rANS is used; Table 2 timings mix single-thread and 16-thread numbers. Datasets named Cortex/Cells/Fiber are visualization corpora, not a claim of a new biological reconstruction. “Up to gigabytes per second” is a peak throughput, not a guarantee on CPU-only laptops. Connectomics relevance is as a segmentation-volume codec, not a tracing algorithm.

plain_language_summary: Coloring every voxel in a 3D scan with a cell or material label makes huge files. This paper compresses those label volumes tightly and still draws them in real time on a graphics card.

ocar.opportunity: Flood-filling networks can reconstruct neurons from synaptic-resolution EM, but stock pipelines are too slow and proofreading-heavy for a typical lab reconstructing a larval fly brain.
ocar.challenge: Reproducing FFN-based reconstruction in ordinary laboratory compute settings is difficult because inference, consensus, and agglomeration dominate runtime.
ocar.action: Liu, Zhang, Yu, Sun, Wang, He, Zhao, Zheng, Gong, and Feng, at IEEE EMBC (2023), add acceleration techniques on top of FFN and test them on Drosophila larval brain serial-section EM at synaptic resolution, noting eight worker threads per FFN process and hardware-dependent process counts per GPU.
ocar.resolution: They report that the pipeline significantly reduces inference time versus the FFN baseline and greatly reduces time to reconstruct 3D neuronal morphology, with methods intended to transfer to similar volumes.
ocar.future_work: They plan model pruning and quantization, and they note that consensus and agglomeration may dominate compute at full-brain scale. Optimal process/thread counts should be benchmarked per hardware platform.

summaries.beginner: Tracing every neuron in a larval fruit-fly electron-microscope stack usually takes too long for a small lab. This conference paper speeds up a standard tracing network and says reconstruction finishes much faster on their larval-brain dataset.
summaries.intermediate: At the IEEE EMBC (2023), Liu and colleagues describe FFN acceleration techniques for synaptic-resolution serial-section EM of the Drosophila larval brain. They report substantially reduced inference time versus baseline FFN and faster 3D morphology reconstruction, with multi-process/multi-thread execution (eight worker threads per FFN process in their setup). They argue the recipe can be adapted to similar lab datasets.
summaries.advanced: The abstract and extract do not give a numeric speedup factor, voxel throughput, or proofreading-hour reduction; “significantly reduces” is qualitative. Consensus/agglomeration is flagged as the likely remaining bottleneck at whole-brain scale. Comparison is to FFN baseline, not to later flood-filling or transformer segmenters. Author list in the catalog includes a split given name (“Yixuan; Sun”).

plain_language_summary: Tracing every neuron in a larval fruit-fly electron-microscope stack usually takes too long for a small lab. This conference paper speeds up a standard tracing network and says reconstruction finishes much faster on their larval-brain dataset.

ocar.opportunity: Patch-seq has defined 28 inhibitory MET-types in mouse visual cortex; predicting those types inside a large EM volume would link transcriptomic identity to synapses and myelination.
ocar.challenge: It was unknown how MET-types connect in cortical circuitry, and EM cells lack direct transcriptomic labels.
ocar.action: Gamlin, Schneider-Mizell, Mallory, Elabbady, Gouwens, Williams, Mukora, Dalley, Bodor, Brittain, Buchanan, Bumbarger, Kapner, Kinn, Mahalingam, Seshamani, Takeno, Torres, Yin, Nicovich, Bae, Castro, Dorkenwald, Halageri, Jia, Jordan, Kemnitz, Lee, Li, Lu, Macrina, Mitchell, Mondal, Mu, Nehoran, Popovych, Silversmith, Turner, Wong, Wu, Yu, Berg, Jarsky, Lee, Seung, Zeng, Reid, Collman, da Costa, and Sorensen, on bioRxiv (2023), predict MET-type identity of inhibitory cells in a large-scale EM dataset using morphological features, focusing on somatostatin (Sst) Martinotti cells.
ocar.resolution: EM Martinotti cells were successfully predicted as Sst+ MET-types. Identified MET-types differed in axon myelination and in excitatory targets. MET-4 showed more myelination of the main ascending axon stalk than MET-6; MET-4 had significantly larger output synapses and MET-8 significantly smaller ones, while MET-8 formed significantly more output synapses. They argue morphological features can bridge imaging modalities and that MET-types have distinct connectivity.
ocar.future_work: Whether synapse-size differences map to physiological strength is inferred from excitatory structure–function literature, not measured here for these inhibitory cells. Myelination’s effect on Sst firing is analogized to Pvalb findings.

summaries.beginner: Inhibitory cells in mouse visual cortex have been typed by shape, electricity, and genes. This team guesses those types from electron-microscope shape alone and finds that different predicted types wire to different partners and wrap their axons in different amounts of myelin.
summaries.intermediate: Posted on bioRxiv (2023), Gamlin and colleagues predict inhibitory MET-type identity in a large EM volume using morphology, after Patch-seq defined 28 inhibitory MET-types in mouse V1. Putative Martinotti cells map to Sst+ MET-types. They report type-specific myelination and excitatory targeting, including myelination differences between MET-4 and MET-6 and synapse-size/count differences among MET-4, MET-6, and MET-8. Morphology is offered as a bridge across light, Patch-seq, and EM.
summaries.advanced: MET identity in EM is a prediction from morphology, not dual Patch-seq/EM on the same cells. Significance claims for myelination and synapse size cite supplementary figures; exact n and p-values are not in the selected extract. Synapse-size-to-strength conversion is borrowed from excitatory paired physiology. The work is a preprint on a MICrONS-scale collaboration; completeness of inhibitory reconstruction is not quantified here.

plain_language_summary: Inhibitory cells in mouse visual cortex have been typed by shape, electricity, and genes. This team guesses those types from electron-microscope shape alone and finds that different predicted types wire to different partners and wrap their axons in different amounts of myelin.

ocar.opportunity: A ventral nerve cord connectome can explain why stimulating particular thoracic bristles recruits hind-leg grooming and why the thorax is last in the grooming hierarchy.
ocar.challenge: Thoracic grooming mixes body sweeps and leg rubs, so a command neuron that seems to trigger the whole subroutine might actually command only one half, and competing mechanosensory cues from other body parts must be able to suppress thorax cleaning.
ocar.action: Yoshikawa, Tang, and Simpson, on bioRxiv (2023), identify cholinergic command-like Mago-no-Te (MGT) neurons whose optogenetic activation elicits hind-leg thoracic grooming, then use VNC EM connectome data plus clonal and amputation experiments, and identify GABAergic UMGT1 cells that synapse onto MGT and its premotor partners.
ocar.resolution: MGT commands thoracic sweeps; contact between leg and thorax is required to initiate leg rubbing. UMGT1 receives diverse sensory inputs and, when activated, suppresses thoracic cleaning—offering a mechanism for other body parts to take precedence. They also map premotor circuitry downstream of MGT, including inhibitory feedback that may support rhythmic limb movement.
ocar.future_work: The full behavioral repertoire of notum bristles remains unknown; linking UMGT1 to specific competing sensory channels in intact flies is the natural next test.

summaries.beginner: Flies clean themselves from front to back, and the thorax is last. This paper finds a command cell that starts chest-sweeping with the hind legs, shows that actual touching is needed to start leg-rubbing, and finds an inhibitory cell that can cancel chest cleaning when other itches come first.
summaries.intermediate: Posted on bioRxiv (2023), Yoshikawa, Tang, and Simpson identify a pair of cholinergic command-like neurons, Mago-no-Te (MGT), that drive thoracic grooming by the hind legs. Connectome analysis of the VNC, plus unilateral activation and amputation, shows MGT commands body sweeps while leg–thorax contact is required for rubbing. A pair of GABAergic UMGT1 neurons receives mixed sensory input, synapses onto MGT and premotor elements, and suppresses thoracic cleaning when optogenetically activated. Downstream inhibitory loops are proposed to support rhythmicity.
summaries.advanced: Command-like status is optogenetic and anatomical, not a proof that MGT is necessary for all natural thoracic grooming. Hierarchy via UMGT1 is a proposed mechanism consistent with connectivity and activation, not a full competition assay across all body parts in this extract. Catalog dataset tag is FANC/MANC VNC; which VNC release is used should be checked in the paper. Preprint.

plain_language_summary: Flies clean themselves from front to back, and the thorax is last. This paper finds a command cell that starts chest-sweeping with the hind legs, shows that actual touching is needed to start leg-rubbing, and finds an inhibitory cell that can cancel chest cleaning when other itches come first.

ocar.opportunity: 3D EM reconstructions have revealed specific retinal connections and new computational features, so a focused review can inventory what is known and what is still missing.
ocar.challenge: Retinal circuitry is intricate across layers; many motifs, especially in primate retina across locations, remain incompletely mapped at synapse resolution.
ocar.action: Sawant, Saha, Khoussine, Sinha, and Hoon, in a Frontiers in Ophthalmology mini-review (2023), summarize retinal circuitry and the insights EM connectomics has provided, and they list open questions.
ocar.resolution: They argue that serial EM has mapped new connections and refined existing ones, supporting how retinal neurons establish connections and compute. They highlight remaining gaps in synaptic organization and in primate connectivity motifs across retinal locations.
ocar.future_work: They state that future serial-EM studies are essential to tease apart location-dependent differences in primate retina and other unresolved circuit questions.

summaries.beginner: The retina is a layered computer made of cells whose connections are now being mapped with 3D electron microscopy. This short review says what those maps have taught us and what still needs mapping, especially in primates.
summaries.intermediate: In Frontiers in Ophthalmology (2023), Sawant, Saha, Khoussine, Sinha, and Hoon mini-review EM connectomics of retinal circuits. They summarize how 3D reconstructions clarified layer-specific connections and visual computations, and they emphasize unresolved synaptic organization, including primate motifs across retinal locations, as targets for future serial EM.
summaries.advanced: This is a mini-review without new reconstructions or numeric error rates. Claims about “what EM has taught” are synthetic; specific datasets (mouse vs primate, IPL volumes) should be checked in the cited primary papers. The selected extract is short (~6k characters) and the discussion is brief. Catalog organism is mouse retina, but the review’s scope includes primate gaps.

plain_language_summary: The retina is a layered computer made of cells whose connections are now being mapped with 3D electron microscopy. This short review says what those maps have taught us and what still needs mapping, especially in primates.

ocar.opportunity: Zebrafish is a standard model for nervous-system development and disease; electron microscopy can capture synaptic ultrastructure and, with volume EM, architecture that informs function.
ocar.challenge: Many EM techniques and protocols exist, and suitability depends on the question and tissue, so researchers need a guide rather than a single default method.
ocar.action: Markert, in Development, Growth & Differentiation (2023), reviews EM techniques applied to the zebrafish nervous system, covering synaptic snapshots, connectomic mapping, and volumetric architecture.
ocar.resolution: The review organizes methods by research question and capability, aiming to help groups choose techniques for structure–function and disease studies in zebrafish neurobiology.
ocar.future_work: Choice remains question-dependent; the piece points to work such as Svara et al. on larval-brain synapse-level reconstruction as part of the landscape rather than reproducing those results.

summaries.beginner: Zebrafish are widely used to study brains in health and disease, and electron microscopy can show synapses and whole-circuit layout. This review is a guidebook to which EM methods fit which zebrafish questions.
summaries.intermediate: Markert (Development, Growth & Differentiation, 2023) reviews electron microscopy of the zebrafish nervous system, from synaptic vesicle and membrane dynamics to volumetric reconstructions that make architecture accessible. The stated aim is to match techniques to questions, tissue, and lab capability, including disease-relevant ultrastructure. References in the extract include Svara and colleagues’ automated synapse-level larval-brain reconstruction.
summaries.advanced: This is a review; it does not report a new connectome or benchmark scores. The selected extract’s ending is the reference list, so detailed method comparisons in the full article should be read directly. Catalog dataset tag DS15 zebrafish is the survey’s zebrafish resource pointer, not a claim that this review generated that volume.

plain_language_summary: Zebrafish are widely used to study brains in health and disease, and electron microscopy can show synapses and whole-circuit layout. This review is a guidebook to which EM methods fit which zebrafish questions.

ocar.opportunity: Lobula columnar (LC) neurons in Drosophila each form a glomerulus in a stereotyped central-brain position, so physiology plus connectomics could explain what that map is for.
ocar.challenge: Whether neighboring glomeruli encode related visual features, and whether downstream neurons exploit that arrangement, was unclear.
ocar.action: Klapoetke, Nern, Rogers, Rubin, Reiser, and Card, in Neuron (2022), as described in the catalog abstract, use single-neuron calcium imaging of 10 glomeruli and connectome analysis of downstream integration.
ocar.resolution: They report new detectors for objects smaller than lens resolution (LC18) and for complex line motion (LC25). Glomeruli cluster by looming versus drifting selectivity and are ordered by size tuning into a topographic feature map. Downstream neurons integrate sparse, similar-feature glomerulus combinations.
ocar.future_work: The abstract presents LC neurons as an explicit example of feature detectors arranged to facilitate integration; further cell types beyond the 10 glomeruli are outside this study’s stated scope.

summaries.beginner: In the fruit fly, some visual cells each dump their output into a little knot in a fixed place in the brain. This Neuron paper records those knots and finds they are arranged by what they see—looming versus drifting, and object size—so downstream cells can mix related features.
summaries.intermediate: Klapoetke et al. (Neuron, 2022), as described in the catalog abstract, image 10 LC glomeruli and analyze downstream connectome combinations. They report LC18 as a detector of objects smaller than the lens resolution and LC25 as a complex line-motion detector, spatial clustering by looming versus drifting object motion, topographic size tuning, and sparse downstream mixing biased toward similar features. Summaries here follow the catalog abstract because the associated PDF extract is a different article.
summaries.advanced: The PDF text supplied with pdf_trust=ok is Sager, Pfeiffer, Wu, Pallasdies, Gowers, Ravikumar, Wu, Colón-Ramos, Schreiber, and Clark, “Spatial and morphological organization of mitochondria in neurons across a connectome” (Science, 2026), not Klapoetke et al. 2022. Claims above are taken only from the catalog abstract. Independent reading of the Neuron paper is needed for stimuli, n, and connectivity matrices. Do not treat mitochondrial morphology results as part of this work.

plain_language_summary: In the fruit fly, some visual cells each dump their output into a little knot in a fixed place in the brain. This Neuron paper records those knots and finds they are arranged by what they see—looming versus drifting, and object size—so downstream cells can mix related features.

ocar.opportunity: If calcium activity can predict who synapses on whom and how strongly, connectomes might be inferred in animals where EM reconstruction is incomplete.
ocar.challenge: EM reconstructions exist for only a few organisms, and synaptic strength is usually estimated indirectly from size and number rather than from functional influence.
ocar.action: Yuan, Liu, Zhao, Wang, Gu, Rong, Lai, Chen, Xin, Niu, Xiang, Huo, Li, and Fang, in Journal of Neural Engineering (2022), train a graph network on C. elegans calcium activity to predict connections and estimate strength, including excitatory versus inhibitory sign.
ocar.resolution: They report reliable prediction of C. elegans synaptic connections and strength as a composite of type, size, transmitters/receptors, and activity dependence. Chemical synaptic strength is described as almost linearly positively correlated with electrical synaptic strength, and one neuron’s influence on another as nonlinearly related to the number of intervening neurons.
ocar.future_work: They present the model as a data-driven route to reconstruct connectomes in more complex systems; whether the same mapping holds outside C. elegans is not shown here.

summaries.beginner: Instead of only looking at electron-microscope pictures of worm synapses, this study uses calcium activity and a graph neural network to guess which cells connect and how strongly. It also tries to say whether a connection is excitatory or inhibitory.
summaries.intermediate: In Journal of Neural Engineering (2022), Yuan and colleagues propose a graph network that predicts C. elegans synapses and estimates strength from calcium activity. They report that predicted strengths reflect a mix of anatomical and biochemical factors, that excitability versus inhibition can be identified, that chemical and electrical synaptic strengths are almost linearly positively correlated, and that influence between neurons relates nonlinearly to path length. They argue this could scale to more complex nervous systems.
summaries.advanced: “Reliable prediction” is the authors’ claim; numeric AUCs or precision/recall are not in the selected extract (ending is references/ORCID). Strength is a model latent, not a paired voltage-clamp measurement. Correlation between chemical and electrical estimates could partly reflect shared activity drive. Generalization beyond C. elegans is aspirational. Catalog dataset is the White+ worm connectome used as comparison structure.

plain_language_summary: Instead of only looking at electron-microscope pictures of worm synapses, this study uses calcium activity and a graph neural network to guess which cells connect and how strongly. It also tries to say whether a connection is excitatory or inhibitory.

ocar.opportunity: Drosophila’s small circadian network shares motifs with mammalian clocks, so a synapse-level map of lateral neurons (LNs) could explain functional pacemaker classes.
ocar.challenge: Anatomical and physiological LN subclasses were known, but whether they are distinct connectomic types, and whether non-clock cells sit at highly coupled nodes, was untested at synapse resolution.
ocar.action: Shafer, Gutierrez, Li, Mildenhall, Spira, Marty, Lazar, and Fernández, on bioRxiv (2022), assess synaptic connectivity of LN clock neuron classes in the fly, claiming what they believe is the first comprehensive connectomic analysis of a circadian neuronal network.
ocar.resolution: Previously identified anatomical and functional LN subclasses correspond to distinct connectomic types. A small number of clock-cell subtypes are highly synaptically coupled nodes. The authors infer that neurons lacking molecular timekeeping likely play integral roles in the timekeeping network.
ocar.future_work: How those non-clock nodes contribute to robustness of behavioral rhythms is the implied physiological follow-up. The extract’s latter pages are identifier tables rather than a full discussion.

summaries.beginner: Fruit-fly clock cells keep daily time, but they need to be wired to each other—and maybe to cells that are not clocks themselves. This preprint maps those synapses and says known clock-cell groups are also distinct wiring types, with a few highly connected hubs.
summaries.intermediate: Posted on bioRxiv (2022), Shafer, Gutierrez, Fernández and colleagues analyze Drosophila lateral neuron (LN) clock-cell connectivity. They report that established anatomical/functional LN subclasses are distinct connectomic types and that a few subtypes are highly coupled nodes, suggesting neurons without molecular clocks may still sit inside the timekeeping network. They contrast the fly’s small network with the mammalian SCN.
summaries.advanced: “First comprehensive connectomic analysis of a circadian neuronal network” is an authorship claim. Quantitative synapse matrices are not in the selected extract (the tail is neuron-ID tables). “Neurons lacking molecular timekeeping” as integral nodes is an inference from coupling, not a clock-gene expression census in this snippet. Preprint; later journal version (if any) should be checked for updates.

plain_language_summary: Fruit-fly clock cells keep daily time, but they need to be wired to each other—and maybe to cells that are not clocks themselves. This preprint maps those synapses and says known clock-cell groups are also distinct wiring types, with a few highly connected hubs.

ocar.opportunity: C. elegans now has anatomical connectomes from multiple animals plus brain-wide calcium imaging, so one can ask how a static wiring diagram supports flexible behavior.
ocar.challenge: Functional coupling among neurons varies with context even when anatomy is stereotyped; the mapping from connectome to dynamics is therefore incomplete without neuromodulation.
ocar.action: Flavell and Gordus, in Current Opinion in Neurobiology (2022), review EM stereotypy, brain-wide imaging, and circuit studies showing that neuromodulators acting over long timescales set persistent behavioral states by changing functional coupling.
ocar.resolution: They argue that dynamic coupling lets multiple behavioral states live in a physically stereotyped connectome, with serotonin, dopamine, and more than 200 neuropeptides as a large modulatory overlay. Evolutionary change can retune existing functional relationships rather than add neurons.
ocar.future_work: They call for a neuromodulatory connectome and brain-wide dynamics in defined modulatory states, building on subset-circuit mechanisms already reviewed.

summaries.beginner: The worm’s wiring diagram looks almost the same from animal to animal, yet the worm behaves differently depending on hunger and other states. This review explains that chemical messengers can retune which wired-up cells actually work together.
summaries.intermediate: In Current Opinion in Neurobiology (2022), Flavell and Gordus review how C. elegans combines a stereotyped anatomical connectome with flexible functional connectivity. They synthesize multi-animal EM maps, brain-wide calcium imaging, and circuit studies in which neuromodulators set persistent states. They emphasize serotonin and dopamine conservation and note more than 200 encoded neuropeptides as future mapping targets.
summaries.advanced: This is a review; it does not present a new whole-animal reconstruction. “Many C. elegans animals” refers to cited EM studies, not a number re-derived here. Functional coupling claims inherit the resolution and cell identity of the imaging papers reviewed. The neuromodulatory connectome is a stated goal, not a completed resource in this article.

plain_language_summary: The worm’s wiring diagram looks almost the same from animal to animal, yet the worm behaves differently depending on hunger and other states. This review explains that chemical messengers can retune which wired-up cells actually work together.

ocar.opportunity: Targeted reconstruction of synapses and mitochondria from serial-section EM can reveal structural plasticity after learning without reconstructing an entire volume by hand.
ocar.challenge: Full ssEM analysis is computationally costly; fear-conditioning effects on mitochondrial number/size and on multi-contact synapses in auditory cortex needed a scalable detector.
ocar.action: Liu, Qi, Chen, Li, Hong, Ma, Li, Shen, Liu, Kong, Zhai, Xie, Han, and Yang, in Cell Reports (2022), as described in the catalog abstract, apply a Region-CNN deep-learning method to identify, segment, and reconstruct synapses and mitochondria in mouse auditory cortex after fear conditioning.
ocar.resolution: After reconstructing over 135,000 mitochondria and 160,000 synapses, they report that fear conditioning increases mitochondrial number but decreases size, and promotes multi-contact synapses (one bouton onto multiple postsynaptic sites from different dendrites). Modeling indicates that configuration increases information-storage capacity of new synapses by over 50%.
ocar.future_work: The abstract presents the method as yielding insight into cellular plasticity; causal tests of the storage-capacity model are outside the stated EM survey.

summaries.beginner: After mice learn a fear, their auditory cortex synapses and mitochondria change shape and number. This paper uses a deep-learning helper on electron-microscope stacks to count those changes at huge scale.
summaries.intermediate: Liu et al. (Cell Reports, 2022), as described in the catalog abstract, use a Region-CNN to reconstruct synapses and mitochondria in ssEM of mouse auditory cortex after fear conditioning. They report >135,000 mitochondria and >160,000 synapses, increased mitochondrial number with decreased size, more multi-contact synapses, and a model in which that configuration raises information-storage capacity of new synapses by over 50%. Summaries here follow the catalog abstract because the associated PDF extract is a different article.
summaries.advanced: The PDF text supplied with pdf_trust=ok is Zhao, Ardiel, Nurrish, and Kaplan, “Trans-synaptic linking of calcium channels and post-synaptic receptors at a dyadic synapse” (PNAS, 2026), a C. elegans motor-neuron study, not Liu et al. 2022. Counts and the 50% storage claim are taken only from the catalog abstract. Independent reading of the Cell Reports paper is required for accuracy metrics, animal n, and the storage model. Do not treat UNC-40/DCC or ACR-12 results as part of this work.

plain_language_summary: After mice learn a fear, their auditory cortex synapses and mitochondria change shape and number. This paper uses a deep-learning helper on electron-microscope stacks to count those changes at huge scale.

ocar.opportunity: Skeletons of segmented neurons are needed for analysis, visualization, and error correction once connectomic volumes reach hundreds of terabytes.
ocar.challenge: Existing thinning methods are often biology-agnostic, scale poorly with voxel count, or both, and they can be thrown off by bubbles (mislabeled interior pockets) and missing soma anchors.
ocar.action: Matejek, Franzmeyer, Wei, Wang, Zhao, Palágyi, Lichtman, and Pfister, in IEEE Transactions on Medical Imaging (2022), remove biologically infeasible bubbles, detect somata with a CNN, then apply synapse-aware topological thinning so endpoints nearly match synapses, while estimating neurite width and geodesic synapse-to-soma distance.
ocar.resolution: On more than 1,250 neurons and fragments from three species they report 47.5% and 62.8% accuracy improvements on width and geodesic distance versus baselines, over one million voxels per second per CPU, and linear scalability. Data-parallel steps increase throughput. Example neurons spanning 270 billion voxels are illustrated.
ocar.future_work: The method still depends on upstream segmentation and synapse detections; residual biological errors in those inputs will propagate.

summaries.beginner: Once a computer has colored in all the neurons, you still need stick-figure centerlines for measuring and checking them. This paper builds those skeletons in a way that respects cell bodies and synapses and runs fast on huge volumes.
summaries.intermediate: In IEEE TMI (2022), Matejek and colleagues present biologically aware skeletonization: bubble removal, CNN soma detection, and synapse-aware thinning with nearly one-to-one endpoint–synapse correspondence. They estimate neurite width and synapse-to-soma geodesic distance with 47.5% and 62.8% accuracy gains over baselines, tested on >1,250 neurons/fragments from three species at >10^6 voxels/s/CPU with linear scaling.
summaries.advanced: The 47.5% and 62.8% figures are relative accuracy improvements on geometric properties, not segmentation F1. “Three different species” are not named in the selected extract’s abstract block (figures/citations mention Drosophila, among others). Performance inherits synapse and soma detector quality. Linear CPU scaling is reported for their pipeline split, not a guarantee on every cluster file system.

plain_language_summary: Once a computer has colored in all the neurons, you still need stick-figure centerlines for measuring and checking them. This paper builds those skeletons in a way that respects cell bodies and synapses and runs fast on huge volumes.

ocar.opportunity: C. elegans neurons are anatomically simple, but synapse coordinates in the connectome make it possible to test whether even single neurites support local computation via clustered contacts.
ocar.challenge: It was unclear whether synapse positions are random, forced by anatomy, or clustered in ways that would allow compartmentalized integration, reciprocal feedback, and coordinated downstream drive.
ocar.action: Ruach, Ratner, Emmons, and Zaslaver, on bioRxiv (2022), analyze chemical-synapse coordinates along neurites, compare them to random and anatomy-constrained nulls, and examine mutual synapses and triple-neuron motifs.
ocar.resolution: Synapses tend to cluster beyond those nulls. In mutually synapsing pairs, opposite-polarity connections cluster separately, suggesting localized positive versus negative feedback. In triples, layouts may support local integration of sensory inputs onto interneurons and coordinated activation of motor neurons. Interneurons are the primary cells implementing local compartmentalized activity, consistent with prior imaging.
ocar.future_work: Functional tests of the proposed local computations remain to be done at the scale of the statistical motifs; several cited studies already show compartmentalized activity in identified interneurons.

summaries.beginner: Worm neurons are simple cables, so it was easy to assume they mix all their inputs together. This study shows synapses sit in clumps, which could let different bits of the same cable do different mini-computations.
summaries.intermediate: Posted on bioRxiv (2022), Ruach, Ratner, Emmons, and Zaslaver use C. elegans synapse coordinates to show that chemical synapses cluster along neurites more than random or purely anatomical placement would predict. Mutual connections of opposite polarity cluster separately. Triple-neuron layouts are enriched for nearby sensory inputs onto interneurons and for nearby outputs onto motor neurons, which they interpret as local integration and coordinated motor drive. Interneurons are highlighted as the main compartmentalized processors.
summaries.advanced: Clustering is a spatial statistic on the then-available connectome, not a new EM volume. Functional roles (integration, correlated motor output) are inferred from geometry plus cited physiology, not measured here for each motif. Gap junctions are outside the chemical-synapse focus. The work is a preprint. Null-model details should be checked in the methods for how “anatomical constraints” were implemented.

plain_language_summary: Worm neurons are simple cables, so it was easy to assume they mix all their inputs together. This study shows synapses sit in clumps, which could let different bits of the same cable do different mini-computations.

ocar.opportunity: An ultra-high-resolution, iteratively annotated EM membrane dataset could expose where today’s segmenters still fail relative to humans, unlike ISBI 2012 where deep learning already neared human scores.
ocar.challenge: State-of-the-art connectomics segmenters still lag scientific need; existing public sets may be too easy or too low-resolution to show the remaining gap.
ocar.action: Shi, Wang, Li, He, Sheng, Ma, Du, Jiang, and Huang, in Frontiers in Computational Neuroscience (2022), release U-RISC (2.18 nm/pixel), run an open competition, perform attribution analysis of networks, and then integrate methods into a stronger benchmark.
ocar.resolution: Competition performance remained well below human level (unlike ISBI 2012). Attribution analysis indicated that U-RISC requires a larger spatial context around a pixel to decide membrane membership. Integrating available methods raised the benchmark to 0.67, about 10% above the competition leader’s 0.61. Data and code are public.
ocar.future_work: They offer suggestions for algorithm development based on the context-window finding; closing the remaining human–machine gap on 2.18 nm data is the open challenge.

summaries.beginner: This team published extremely zoomed-in electron-microscope pictures of cell membranes and ran a contest. Today’s best programs still lose to humans on this set, unlike an older easier contest.
summaries.intermediate: In Frontiers in Computational Neuroscience (2022), Shi and colleagues present U-RISC, an iteratively annotated cell-membrane EM dataset at 2.18 nm/pixel. An open competition showed a large remaining gap to human performance, in contrast to ISBI 2012. Attribution analysis suggests models need a wider neighborhood to classify a pixel as membrane. Combining methods yielded a benchmark of 0.67 versus the leader’s 0.61. GitHub hosts data and code.
summaries.advanced: The 0.67 and 0.61 figures are the authors’ reported scores on their metric; the extract does not define the metric in the selected tail (author contributions/supplement captions). “Largest cell membrane-annotated EM dataset” is an authorship claim. Attribution analysis is model-dependent. Downsampling effects are discussed in an appendix figure; users should not assume 2.18 nm models transfer to 4–8 nm connectomics volumes without retesting.

plain_language_summary: This team published extremely zoomed-in electron-microscope pictures of cell membranes and ran a contest. Today’s best programs still lose to humans on this set, unlike an older easier contest.

ocar.opportunity: FlyBrainLab can host not only anatomy but a programmable account of circuit function, so English queries and executable motifs could sit on connectome/synaptome data.
ocar.challenge: Even the relatively small Drosophila brain has circuit complexity that is hard to model; anatomy ontologies do not capture functional logic, odorant space, or massive local feedback.
ocar.action: Lazar, Turkcan, and Zhou, on bioRxiv (2021), present a programmable ontology integrated with FlyBrainLab, NeuroNLP++ for free-form English circuit construction, an odorant-space model for antennal sensory circuits, and a library for antennal-lobe glomeruli with dense local feedback (example: DM4 and DL5 coupled by LN1–LN3).
ocar.resolution: They demonstrate interactive exploration of massive feedback loops in the antennal lobe, including two-glomerulus constructs and PN responses on grids of concentration-modulated affinities. The ontology is meant to model circuit motifs and to explore their functional logic programmatically.
ocar.future_work: Extending the same executable abstractions beyond early olfaction is implied; the extract’s ending is an evaluation protocol for two glomeruli plus acknowledgments, not a whole-brain function map.

summaries.beginner: Having a fly wiring diagram is not the same as having a working model of what the circuits do. This preprint adds a programmable language, a search box for English questions, and demo models of smell circuits full of feedback loops.
summaries.intermediate: Posted on bioRxiv (2021), Lazar, Turkcan, and Zhou extend Drosophila brain ontologies into a programmable layer inside FlyBrainLab. NeuroNLP++ builds circuits from English queries anchored on connectome/synaptome data and literature. They add an odorant-space model for antennal sensory neurons and methods for antennal-lobe circuits dominated by local feedback, demonstrated with a circuit library including coupled DM4 and DL5 glomeruli.
summaries.advanced: This is infrastructure plus example models, not a claim that antennal-lobe function is solved. Feedback-loop evaluations use specified LN connectivity assumptions (e.g., excitatory LN1/LN2→LN3) that should not be read as the only biological configuration. NeuroNLP++ coverage depends on underlying datasets and literature indexing. Preprint; “all rights reserved” banner in the extract.

plain_language_summary: Having a fly wiring diagram is not the same as having a working model of what the circuits do. This preprint adds a programmable language, a search box for English questions, and demo models of smell circuits full of feedback loops.

ocar.opportunity: Hourglass analysis asks whether a few intermediate nodes mediate paths from many inputs to many outputs; adding synapse weights could change which neurons look like the waist of the C. elegans connectome.
ocar.challenge: Unweighted hourglass methods can miss pathways that are heavily used, and male versus hermaphrodite connectomes plus older versus newer edge sets disagree on core nodes.
ocar.action: Batta, Yao, Sabrin, and Dovrolis, in PLOS ONE (2021), develop a weighted hourglass framework (multi-edge transformation, MET) and apply it to hermaphrodite and male C. elegans structural connectomes, comparing MET with unweighted analysis (UNW) and datasets from White-era maps versus Cook et al. weighted maps.
ocar.resolution: Weighted analysis yields a smaller core and a more visible hourglass than unweighted analysis. Most core nodes in the male concentrate in sex organs, versus the head in the hermaphrodite. Unweighted metrics are higher on the older dataset than on Cook et al.’s unweighted graphs, consistent with added edges being weaker; weighted MET metrics behave differently.
ocar.future_work: They argue that ignoring weights hides network patterns; applying the same weighted hourglass to other connectomes is the natural extension.

summaries.beginner: In a worm, many sensors and muscles might talk through a small set of in-between cells, like sand in an hourglass. This paper counts those paths using synapse size and number, and finds different “waist” cells in males and hermaphrodites.
summaries.intermediate: In PLOS ONE (2021), Batta, Yao, Sabrin, and Dovrolis introduce a weighted hourglass-analysis framework and apply it to C. elegans. Compared with unweighted analysis, the weighted (MET) core is smaller and hourglass scores are stronger. Male cores concentrate in sex organs; hermaphrodite cores in the head. Differences versus the White et al. unweighted hermaphrodite map and Cook et al. weighted/unweighted sexed connectomes are discussed, including weaker extra edges reducing unweighted hourglass strength.
summaries.advanced: The catalog journal field lists bioRxiv, but the PDF and DOI (10.1371/journal.pone.0249846) are PLOS ONE; this summary follows the published article. Core membership depends on path-weight definitions in MET versus UNW; it is not a unique neuronal “bottleneck” list. Hourglass metrics (H-score, cumulative path coverage) are plotted in figures; exact numeric H-scores are not copied from the extract. Functional use of core neurons is not measured here.

plain_language_summary: In a worm, many sensors and muscles might talk through a small set of in-between cells, like sand in an hourglass. This paper counts those paths using synapse size and number, and finds different “waist” cells in males and hermaphrodites.

ocar.opportunity: A glutaraldehyde-resistant clearing method would let the same labeled neurons be imaged from whole-brain light microscopy down to EM synapses.
ocar.challenge: Standard clearing is poorly compatible with EM fixation, and rare synaptic contacts are hard to find without multi-scale targeting.
ocar.action: Furuta, Yamauchi, Okamoto, Takahashi, Kakuta, Ishida, Takenaka, Yoshida, Uchiyama, Koike, Isa, Isa, and Hioki, in iScience (2021), introduce ScaleSF and successive LM/EM imaging, demonstrated on mouse striatofugal, mouse callosal, and marmoset corticostriatal projections, including APEX2 DAB-Ni²⁺ labeling and FIB-SEM.
ocar.resolution: They report seamless integration of macroscopic, mesoscopic, microscopic, and EM scales, enabling simultaneous interrogation of circuit structure and synaptic connectivity and zooming in on scarce contacts. Highlights list successive LM/EM in optically cleared tissue.
ocar.future_work: The methods section in the extract points to STAR Protocols-style resources; broader cell-type panels and fully automated targeting are implied next steps rather than shown as a production pipeline.

summaries.beginner: Seeing a whole brain and then the same cell’s synapses usually requires different preparations. This paper clears tissue in a way that still works for electron microscopy, so researchers can zoom from brain-wide maps down to individual contacts.
summaries.intermediate: In iScience (2021), Furuta, Hioki and colleagues present ScaleSF, a glutaraldehyde-resistant clearing protocol coupled to successive light and electron microscopy. They apply it to mouse striatofugal and callosal systems and to marmoset corticostriatal projections, combining confocal imaging with TEM and FIB-SEM after APEX2-based DAB-Ni²⁺ labeling. The stated payoff is multi-scale neuronal imaging from brain to synapse and targeted inspection of scarce contacts.
summaries.advanced: This is a methods/resource paper; quantitative synapse yields and clearing-induced ultrastructure metrics should be read from the full figures (the selected extract ends in STAR Methods headings). Compatibility is demonstrated on three projection systems, not a whole-brain EM connectome. Marmoset inclusion is important for primate translation but is a targeted projection, not cortex-wide mapping.

plain_language_summary: Seeing a whole brain and then the same cell’s synapses usually requires different preparations. This paper clears tissue in a way that still works for electron microscopy, so researchers can zoom from brain-wide maps down to individual contacts.
